On section 14,

Pursuant to notice, I move, in the absence of Mr. McCarthy, that the following be added as section 14:
The company may lease or otherwise acquire coal mines and coal mining rights, and wcrk, develop, operate and turn to account all such coal mines and coal mining rights held by the company.

This clause I took objection to in the committee, but my attention was called to the fact that we had given the same right to other railway companies who contemplated operating in that country, where coal is so very plentiful, in order to get traffic. While I still regard it as objectionable, it is not nearly so objectionable as a Bill which preceded it, in regard to a company which proposed to go into the United States and purchase coal. In that case there was really a monopoly of the coal business by the Grand Trunk railway. You might buy coal from a mine owner, but you could not ^et the Grand Trunk railway to bring the coal across the line for you unless it was bought from the parties with whom they were operating. But in the Northwest there is not likely to

be a monopoly of that kind, because coal is so plentiful.
I wa6 opposed to the clause on principle, but if it has been arranged between the parties, I do not think I should interfere.

I think we. had better let it pass. It was explained in the committee pretty fully. In the west the railway companies practically all own coal areas, and operate them in connection with their traffic. It may be that in the years to come we shall have to cancel all these rights by legislation if they are abused. If it should happen that the coal companies and the transportation companies should put their heads together so that where you reduce the freight rates they will add them to the price of coal, it might be necessary to pass legislation in Canada similar to what has been passed in the United States, prohibiting coal companies and railway companies from being one and the same people.

Under what regulations are coal mines operated in the west? With us they are operated under very stringent laws and regulations adopted by the local legislature. The running of a coal mine is a pretty important thing, and I think it is rather dangerous to allow these mines to be operated without any regulation, or to allow any company to own and operate a coal mine. Coal mines should be operated under regulations that would safeguard the lives and health and general safety of the coal miners.

All that this House is professing to do is to incorporate a company, and to give it power to operate mines. How those mines should be operated would be a matter of local jurisdiction if they come within local jurisdiction, of Dominion jurisdiction if they come within that. We do not interfere with the right the Dominion would have, in the place of a provincial government, to regulate how the mines should be worked. If we incorporate a company and give it power to undertake some manufacturing enterprise, we do not, therefore, exempt it from the right the province would have to regulate how its industry should be carried on. All we do is to give this company a right to do a certain thing, and that must be done in conformity with the law.

I do not think my hon. friend's knowledge of everything in heaven above, on the earth beneath and in the waters under the earth, includes a knowledge of how to run a coal mine. If the coal belongs to the province, it may have the right to make regulations; if it does not, it has no right to make regulations as to operating.
Nobody said it had.
My hon. friend says this company will be given the right to own and operate a coal mine, and the local government may eome in and make regulations.
Not at all.

I ask, who is going to make them? We have no law governing this point, so far as I know. The operating of a coal mine is a scientific subject. I have never heard of giving, in this general way in a Railway Act, the right to own and operate coal mines in any province. I am told that the local legislature would have no control over this company or its operations. I am inquiring whether there is any law on the subject. I would like to see the mining laws of this country made as uniform as possible. We have excellent mining laws in the province of Nova Scotia, and 1 would like to see them in force wherever there is a coal mine. I presume that there are good mining laws in British Columbia and in Alberta, and I would like to know that this right to operate a coal mine is subject to the laws of the province where the coal mine is situated.

I have no intention of opposing this clause. Practically all the other railway companies who are doing business in Alberta own coal mines and large tracts of coal land; but I want to point out to the Minister of Railways that what he thinks may possibly exist in a short time is very likely to exist. All the large railway companies own, and some of them operate, coal mines in Alberta, and those who are not operating are preparing to operate. These big railway companies have also bought out practically all the coal mines in British Columbia. Therefore, we are very likely to have in the west the same condition that exists in Pennsylvania and Ohio, where the railway companies own so much of the coal lands that they can dictate terms to everybody else who owns coal lands, and who does not happen to own a railway in connection with them. The point raised by my hon. friend from Cape Breton I think is a very reasonable point, but in Alberta and Saskatchewan, while the Dominion government own the coal lands, the local governments have control of the working and inspection of the mines, and I have always felt that as the local governments have all the expense of these services, it would be better if they had full control and received whatever royalties there are on coal lands. They would thus be in a better position to look after the safety of the working of the mines. The very position feared by the Minister of Railways is likely to arise in the near future and we should be very careful in granting

the right to these railway companies to own and operate large coal mines for fear that others who have invested in coal mines may be put out of business, because they cannot compete with mines owned by the same people who own the railways.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I want to support in every particular what my hon. friend has just said in regard to the undesirability, in the public interest, of a railway company being also an owner of coal mines. While the same men may own the railways and the mines, if they own them under the one organization neither the local government nor the Dominion government can control their operations as effectually as if they were separate concerns. The situation which the Minister of Railways fears must be dealt with by drastic action if it arises. It will arise in the future if it is permitted, and the time to stop it is now and not hereafter. It strikes me that as this charter is for an electric railway, it is reasonable to say that the precedent in regard to steam railways does not apply. It is evident that the coal mine owner who also owns a railway is in a more advantageous position than the coal mine owner who does not. It is in the public interest that there should be as many separate owners of coal mines as possible and therefore when you give a special advantage to the owner of one coal mine because he owns a railway you enable him to monopolize the coal mines which are tributary to that railway, you put the other owners at a disadvantage and put the general public at a disadvantage to that same degree. I cannot allow this charter to pass without entering the most emphatic protest I can against the principle of chartering railways and coal mines together as in this particular case.
This railway may be operated by electricity, steam or other power. Will that alter the minister's opinion?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That makes no difference in my estimation as to the disadvantage of the owner of the transportation also owning the coal whether the transportation is by steam or electricity.

It may be a steam railway before it is completed. I agree with much of what the minister has said with regard to the advisability of keeping the coal lands separate from any great corporations. I believe what the minister has said will likely take place within a few years and that the railway companies have monopolized too much of our coal lands. With regard to this Bill I feel that we have already created a precedent in the west, we have granted several charters and several companies have secured control of coal mines. I understand a compromise has been arrived at in reference to this Bill, Mr. TURRIFF.
and I think it would be hard to create a new precedent.

In the Railway Committee the point was brought out that if a new railway like this is limited to the operation of the small area of coal land required to furnish its motive power the cost of producing the coal will be increased as compared with the cost of operations on a larger scale, and that this will increase the cost of operation of the railway with a consequent increase in the cost of freight to the public. I agree that if the day has come when the railway companies control the coal we cannot move too soon. The minister will see that if we refuse this right the same individuals may still own the coal and the railway, may have their offices side by side, and the result .to the public would be the same as if they were given the powers asked under this Act. I hope the minister will see that it is really in the interest of the public as well as of the company that the company should be allowed to operate a sufficient amount of coal lands to produce coal at the least possible expense and thus save coal rates.

The argument -of my hon. friend (Mr. Northrup) hardly applies. The great trouble experienced by the coal miners in that part of the country is the lack of cars. Often a mine will have orders in hand to keep it going twenty-four hours a day for months, but they cannot get a regular supply of cars, with the result that they may be working only half time. The difficulty is not so much in the matter of freight rates, or in the selling of the coal by the mine owned by the railway at less than the neighbouring mines sell it, but in this lack of a steady supply of cars.
The Railway Commission can regulate that.

They have control in such a matter. But in a country like that, where there is a tremendous traffic in coal-hon. members hardly realize the traffic there is in coal in the Crowsnest Pass, wheTe there are dozens of mines operating-the success of a mine may depend absolutely upon obtaining cars steadily and in fair proportion and at the right time. It is a pretty difficult matter for a railway commission, or anybody else, to regulate the supply of cars if the railway company are interested in putting cars in any particular place. I am not saying they are doing that now. But I do say there is often a shortage of cars, and there is the tendency of which I have spoken. The House cannot be too careful in legislation of this kind.

Admitting eveTy word that the hon. member (Mr. Turriff) says- namely, that the present grievance in the Northwest is the scarcity of cars, we are not going to correct that by preventing the

railway from adding more cars. And if you allow them to operate the mines they will certainly provide more cars.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I wish to repeat what 1 said. My objection to covering the two enterprises with the one charter is not met by stating that the same people may operate the same enterprise under two different charters. I am not learned in the law, but it seems reasonable to believe that, if the two separate enterprises are operated under two separate charters, each enterprise will be more amenable to the legislation necessary to regulate and control it than if one charter covered both. If the railway charter covers coal operations . there is no doubt that in the legislation to protect the rights of the public we should have more difficulty in reaching the coal [DOT] operation than if the coal operation w'ere carried on under a separate charter. What my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) has said in regard to the possible condition as to the supply of cars I do not know that it is any breach of confidence to say, describes a condition which has prevailed and which has been a very serious drawback to the development of the coal industry in the Crowsnest Pass. That is a matter of recorcl. Building an electric railway in some other part of the province of Alberta to develop other coal mines would have no effect on the situation in the Crowsnest Pass as it exists. The necessary effect of the linking together of the two enterprises is to give an undue advantage to the coal enterprise which is linked with the railway over the coal enterprise which is not linked with the railway. The railway is, or ought to be, a common carrier, to carry for everybody on equal terms-that is the purpose of chartering a railway; the railway gets special privileges on the theory that it will act as a common carrier and will deal on terms of equality with parties desiring to ship over it. But it will not act as a common carrier and deal fairly between parties if it is interested in one particular enterprise to which it looks chiefly for its traffic. No railway commission, no governmental control can properly protect the public interest in these cases. I speak strongly on this matter, because the coal interest of Alberta is probably the greatest interest in the Dominion of Canada, and it is an interest on whose proper development the whole prairie country tremendously depends. It is of interest to every man on the prairie that coal shall be produced under competitive conditions and delivered to him at the lowest possible rates of transportation. There is sufficient tendency to secure monopoly now, and this parliament should not let any legislation pass that would in any way tend to increase the possibilities of monopoly.

I would ask the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) if the proper remedy would not be the one suggested by the Minister of Railways and Canals when he said that he intends to build the Hudson Bay railway in order -this is one of his reasons-that Cape Breton coal may be taken up by vessel to Hudson bay and shipped over the railway and delivered to purchasers in western Canada at much lower prices than it can at present be bought for. I see that one of the reasons assigned by the officers of his department for building this railway is that in Edmonton, for instance, where coal is now selling at $9 a ton, he will be able to deliver it, taken all the way from Cape Breton, at $7 a ton.
That argument was seriously presented to the House this afternoon.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know whether my hon. friend (Mr. Haggart, Lanark) is serious or not, but the Northwest is a big country, and, while there is enormous possibility of production of coal-and, indeed, an enormous production of coal-in the western part of Alberta, yet the charges for transportation are such that it is not possible to deliver that coal in the city of Winnipeg in competition with the coal which is brought from the middle of the state of Pennsylvania, shipped by rail to the lake port-Cleveland-carried thence by steamer to Fort William, transhipped again, and carried by rail to Winnipeg. The transportation rates are such that that coal from Pennsylvania is laid down in Winnipeg at such terms as to practically exclude the Alberta coal from Winnipeg market. Now, what is done with the Pennsylvania coal may, as far as I am aware, be done with the Nova Scotia coal. I am not familiar with the circumstances, but I do not see any greater difficulty in one case than in the other.

Does not the hon. minister (Mr. Oliver) believe that that condition is largely due to the fact that the coal in Pennsylvania is anthracite, while the coal from the west is bituminous, and, therefore, not of equal quality?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) says does not apply, because there is anthracite, as he knows, in the Rocky mountains.
But not of the same quality.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But it is anthracite, and is mined and put on the market under very favourable conditions. But the same applies not only to anthracite, but to the whole coal supply.

But the minister knows that if a party goes to a dealer in Winni-

peg and buys coal he is willing to pay $2 or sometimes $3 more for the Pennsylvania anthracite than for the western bituminous coal, because the heating qualities of it are much better.

The hon. gentleman is altogether wrong as to the heating quality of Pennsylvania, or Virginia, or Ohio bituminous coal being higher than that of the bituminous coal of Alberta; the opposite is the fact. Take the coal from a number of the mines in the Crowsnest Pass, and you will find it high in steam producing qualities, higher than the ordinary bituminous coal that comes from Pennsylvania, as the Minister of the Interior has said. Hundreds of thousands of tons of bituminous coal come in from the eastern United States to Winnipeg, and many of the railroads use American coal for one or two divisions west of Winnipeg, simply because the freight rates are cheaper, and they find it cheaper to use that coal than to bring coal from western Alberta or British Columbia, where the better quality of steam coal can be got.

I wish to tell the hon. gentleman that when I was in Winnipeg some years ago, and I met a gentleman-who was buying a lot of coal from Pennsylvania for which he was prepared to pay $12 a ton, while he could get Canadian coal for $9 a ton. I asked him why he was paying so much more for the Pennsylvania coal, and he said that it was because it was richer in heat producing power.

1 agree with the arguments of the Minister of the Interior, but I cannot agree with his conclusion as to what would happen if we deprived this company of the power of operating coal mines. Now the conditions are such as the minister has stated with reference to railways giving privileges to particular coal mining companies in the way of cars. If that applies to all railway companies who are operating there now, and have the privilege to operate coal mines, and if this railway becomes a competitive railway to the present system, why should you not give the same privileges to this railway? It may be all right to take these privileges away from companies , but I think it should be done at the same time with each and all of them, and that until then this company should have the same privileges as others are enjoying. If they are going to be a competitor in getting low railway rates, they must have the same opportunities in conducting their business.
On section 15,

Before the Bill is reported, I would like to comment on the remarks of the hon. gentleman with reference Mr. SPROULE.
to this clause being the same clause that has been in other Bills that we have put through that we should pass this Bill. I do not agree with that? I am not opposing this Bill now, because it is an arrangement between the parties, the Alberta government and the promoters, but otherwise I would oppose it, because I have opposed in the committee all clauses such as this, and I intend to oppose them. It does not make any difference to me that the charters were given with these clauses in that should not have been given; that is no reason why we should continue to give them.

The same thing is true with regard to passenger business. While the Intercolonial railway had a rate per passenger per mile of 1 -691 cents, the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario had a Tate of 2.485. Here was a difference in favour of the latter of 48-1 per cent. I want to bring that difference clearly before the House, and particularly those members from other parts of Canada, because I believe they do not understand the difficulties of managing a government road of this length and under the peculiar conditions and circumstances surrounding it. The rates on the Intercolonial railway are so much less than those on other roads, that the two cannot fairly be compared as to receipts owing to the difference in the conditions. The revenue quality of our freight is lower, and consequently, our rates are lower than those of any ocher road in Canada.
Are the rates on the Intercolonial railway from St. John and Halifax to Montreal any lower than those on the Canadian Pacific railway?

The rates from St. John to Montreal on the Intercolonial railway are the same as those on the Canadian Pacific railway, but we have to haul the traffic 250 miles for nothing, because our route is 250 miles longer.

The minister made the statement that the rates on the Canadian Pacific railway are higher than those on the Intercolonial railway; but I understand that the rates from St. John to Montreal, and the rates from Montreal to St. John, for both passenger and freight, on both lines are exactly the same.

That only confirms my argument. I have been showing that per ton per mile and per passenger per mile our rates are lower; and one of the difficulties under which we operate is what my hon. friend points out, that we have a haul 250 miles longer than that of the Canadian Pacific railway from St. John to Montreal, and get only the same rate.
When the Canadian Pacific railway runs from St. John to Halifax, who gets the traffic?
We get the local traffic between St. John and Halifax.
Perhaps I do not make myself clear. If a passenger wishes to go from St. John to Montreal, he gets the same rate whether he goes by the Intercolonial railway or the Canadian Pacific railway?
Yes.

If you like to haul him around by Moncton, that is no fault of the Canadian Pacific railway. If the Canadian Pacific railway takes the passenger from Halifax to Montreal, how far does it haul him for nothing? You get the money.
No, we make an arrangement by which they pay us so much for hauling the traffic.
How much do they give you back?

I cannot say at the moment. At all events, my hon. friend has made my point clear, that we have to carry the traffic 250 miles farther, or 50 per cent farther than the Canadian Pacific railway for exactly the same rate. That is one of the difficulties I have been explaining, and I am glad that my hon. friend has brought it out so well. Now, I come to the question of the cost per train mile, and I will try to make a fair comparison by taking the cost on the three railways, the Canadian Pacific railway, the Grand Trunk railway and the Canadian Northern railway.
It might be said, and very frequently is, that the Intercolonial railway is conducted with great extravagance and an utter disregard of sound railway methods. The Canadian Pacific railway, for example, is popularly understood to acquire large net earnings by economical administration.

while the Intercolonial railway is believed to have occasional deficits because it is conducted in a wasteful way. In short, it is asserted that the Canadian Pacific is run on business principles, while the Intercolonial is not.
Is there any way of determining relative economy in the conduct of railways? There is. Look at it as you may, no matter from what standpoint, all the operations of a railway come down to one thing-the running of trains. If you stop the running of trains you stop everything for which a railway pays out money, no matter what it may be. Every penny of operating expenses goes out to that end. Now, the measure of a railway's, operations is expressed in train mileage. Therefore, if you divide the total train mileage into the total operating expenses you have a figure which tells you the cost of running a train one mile.
This cost of running a train one mile is accepted by the entire Tailway world as an absolutely safe and sound standard for measuring economy of administration. The railway which is operated at the lowest cost is certain to have the lowest rate per train mile. It is known to the last farthing what it cost every railway in Canada to run a train one mile during 1910, and taking the cases of those roads to which reference has already been made the figures are as
follow:
Intercolonial	$ 1.300

This comparison is distinctly in favour of the Intercolonial railway. The figures are in each ease taken from the sworn returns of the railway indicated, and are not open to question. They show beyond a doubt that the Intercolonial railway is not wastefully managed; but, in comparison with these roads which are regarded as types of the best conducted in Canada, is carried on in a way highly creditable to those who are in charge of its affairs.
The foregoing observations bring us back to the initial proposition, namely, that the Intercolonial does not earn a large surplus, despite its location and position as the product of confederation, simply because its freight and passenger rates are the lowest in the Dominion. This view, notwithstanding anything that may be asserted to the contrary, will be fully sustained by a comparison of the published freight tariffs of the railways to which allusion has been made.
The comparison I have made is very strongly in favour of the Intercolonial railway; but this much I want to admit, to be perfectly fair, that on account of our comparatively high grades, it may be that we do not haul on an average quite as much
per train as the Canadian Pacific railway. But I think the difference will not be found to be very great; and it is a pleasure for me to announce to the House that such improvement is being made every year that our average number of cars per train is increasing, which shows that we are endeavouring to bring the operation of the road down to the lowest possible cost.
Now, I have pointed out that one of the difficulties under which the Intercolonial railway labours is its low classification of freight. I want to substantiate my contention that per mile the rates authorized by the Board of Railway Commissioners for the Grand Trunk railway and the Canadian Pacific railway are higher than the rates charged by the Intercolonial railway on the same articles. The rates I am about to give are the rates authorized by the Board of Railway Commissioners between Ontario towns, in thickly settled districts, where surely the rate ought to be as low as the rate on the Intercolonial railway, if the Intercolonial railway rate were on a commercial basis, which it is not and never has been. It has been said that for short distances the rates of the Intercolonial railway will be found to be as high as the others. That may possibly be true, but in comparing the Intercolonial railway rates per mile with the rates granted by the Board of Railway Commissioners between Ontario towns, I am going to start at 89 miles.
