This is paid out gf renewal equipment fund, made up of a contribution from the' revenue of $25,000 a month. In this connection, I may say that we have been allowed to establish two accounts, the rail renewal account and the equipment renewal account. On the rail renewal account we have been putting aside $12,500 a month and on the other $25,000 a month. At the end of the year, the balances in these accounts are not handed back to the Receiver General, but we use the funds to renew rails and equipment as necessary. The amount in these accounts does not appear as part of the net revenue, as they are charged against the revenue. I think of asking the House to allow me to establish another account. It would mean practically an insurance account. The ordinary railway is managed on these lines: Where a large fire occurs, they take out of revenue the value of the property as it was before destruction, and, in the construction of the new buildings they charge to capital account only the difference between the value! of the old and the value of the'new. I am' endeavouring to adopt that principle thoroughly on the Intercolonial railway. I had some correspondence with Mr. Knapp, who is chairman of the Interstate Commerce Commission, which has adopted very strict rules in this connection, and he informed ine this was the method the Interstate Commerce Commission adopted, and Mr. Hays of the Grand Trunk tells me the same thing. We had a big fire at Camp-bellton. I had an estimate made of the value of the buildings that were destroyed, and the amount given was $76,000. We purpose enlarging our yards at Campbell-ton, and providing for a connection with the International railway, wmch, we expect, will lead to the handling of quite a lot of traffic. We are changing the location of our yards-I think at the request of the town-and the new yards, station and sidings will cost $250,000. What I propose to do is to pay out of this year's revenue $76,000, the value of the property destroyed. This may be considered a departure. But it is strictly along the line on which railway companies are run, and I think that is the way we ought to run the Intercolonial, even if we do not come out even in so running it. But, as traffic is rapidly increasing, if the Auditor General will allow Mr. GRAHAM.
me, I propose this year to take a further account from net revenue of $100,000 and put it into renewal equipment, so thkt we may have the funds to buy the additional equipment we so much need. In order that there may be no mistake about having authority to do this, I propose, a little later in the session, if I can nossibly do it, with the consent of the Auditor General's Department and the Finance Department, to introduce an amendment to allow us _ to establish and maintain these funds which we have been maintaining to a certain extent without statutory warrant, but with, the consent of the Auditor General. This will make the procedure perfectly legal.
Companies having large fire losses are able to spread these losses over a term of years. An act to be introduced will enable the Intercolonial railway to do the same.
Another question arises: There are differences of opinion as to what ought to be! charged to capital and what ought to be charged to revenue. We have endeavoured to make the line distinct and clear, that whatever a railway company would charge to capital or to revenue, we ought to so charge. And I believe that during the past year, the Intercolonial has actually leaned backwards in this matter and has charged several things to revenue that a railway company would have charged to capital, and would be authorized to charge to capital under the Interstate Commerce rules. Possibly I may introduce a measure to make clear the distinction between revenue and capital expenditure and to give us authority to say which is revenue and which is capital should any question arise between the Audit Department and the board of managers. At the end of this year we will have a little money left, by the looks of things. I am not prepared to say so absolutely, but from the figures I have in my hands, and those I have been able to see, if we were not to take the $76,000 for Camp-bellton, and if we were not to ask for the other extra $100,000 on equipment and renewal account, which I am going to ask for, if I did not make these two deductions, I think possibly at the end of March this year the Intercolonial would show a net revenue of $700,000. It is not the object of the Intercolonial to have a big surplus, we want to give the people a good service, and the situation is such that we never expect to have a very big surplus at the end of the year.
How much will the minister have on equipment account?

If we omitted the diversions at Chatham and George's River, which are practically new lines, the service this year would pay probably all the running expenses and all the capital expenditure of the Intercolonial. We have spent money on revenue account that a company

road would not have to expend on such account but would have charged to capital, and we have not spent one farthing that a company road would not expend.
What do you write off for wear and tear?
It is written off under the same rules and regulations that prevail on company roads under the Interstate Commerce Commission.

The reason I ask that question is that a few days ago I saw a number of locomotives which I thought were ready for the scrap heap, and I was wondering if you regarded them still as an asset. I suppose there were 25 locomotives.

We set aside $300,000 per year to renew equipment. I had an estimate made at one time and I found that our percentage of rolling stock out of commission and waiting for repairs or ready for the scrap heap, as the hon. member says, was a trifle less than the rolling stock of other companies in Canada, by percentage. A good many of our engines are light; we will use some of our lighter engines, that otherwise might not be of much use on the main line, should we take over some of the branch lines where lighter rolling stock can be used.
There is another thing of interest, and that is our relations to the Grand Trunk railway at the city of Montreal. We have been asked what that traffic amounts to. A few years ago an arrangement was made for the Intercolonial to run into Montreal, and by agreement with the Grand Trunk railway their terminals are used, and thejr line is used from Ste. Rosalie into Bonaven-ture station, and we have an arrangement for interchange of traffic. Now the total revenue in 1910 from the freight handed to the Intercolonial by the Grand Trunk, gathered up in Ontario largely-and I want the Ontario members to remember this when they talk of the Intercolonial-that freight in Ontario was gathered up by the Grand Trunk and handed to the Intercolonial, making earnings for the Intercolonial of $908,066.35. The Intercolonial handed to the Grand Trunk freight traffic on which the Intercolonial earned $753,452.28. So the total of the interchange would be about $1,660,000. That arrangement has been a good one. But I want to impress on our Ontario friends that more of that traffic is carried over the Intercolonial east than there is of maritime provinces and Quebec traffic carried from the east to the west. So the advantages that may be gained by having the Intercolonial railway run as cheaply as possible go a little more to the province of Ontario, possibly, than they do to the people through whose territory this railway runs.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: How much has the Intercolonial handed over to the Canadian Pacific railway?

By the arrangement with the Grand Trunk we have to hand all our traffic to them that is not otherwise routed, and they have to do the same with us. The most of our traffic is handed over to the Grand Trunk, Montreal being the junction point. I think there is more freight comes from the west to the east over the Intercolonial than comes from the east to the west.
Now, I want to say a few words about the Prince Edward Island railway. For the nine months ending December 31, 1910, the Prince Edward Island railway had a net loss of $53,294.11. That was a decrease in the loss for nine months over last year of $11,114.93. The Prince Edward Island railway does not pay, never will pay, and no one need ever try to make it pay. It is not the intention of the department to try to make it pay. When the island came into confederation we took over this railway, and it is the duty of the parliament of Canada to give the Prince Edward Island people a good railway service so far as that is possible. Although it is a certain contribution from the federal government to the people of that island, I am prepared, so far as I am concerned, and so long as I am a minister, to advocate a liberal treatment of the people in Prince Edward Island in reference to their transportation facilities.
What was the capital expenditure on that road last year?

Approximately $185,000. We are building a new branch line in Prince Edward Island, which is not yet completed. Last year we spent $206,397.
Now, I have been asked:	What is the
future of the Intercolonial? It stands to reason that it will not be very long, at least it cannot be very long before the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk will come to the government, or to the management of the Intercolonial, and ask to be relieved from their arrangements with us at Montreal to hand us over their traffic. That traffic is very heavy, and they will undoubtedly come to us when the Grand Trunk Pacific is completed and say:	We
want to take our own traffic down from Montreal to LAvis and hand it over to the Grand Trunck Pacific. I do not know what will happen in the years to come when they make that request. I am not prepared to say it will ever be granted; it will not be unless the terms are right. I believe the future of the Intercolonial is bound up in getting an exchange of traffic with a western through line that runs from the Pacific to the Atlantic, and from the Pacific to the St. Lawrence at least. I believe that is what will make the Intercolonial of still



greater benefit to the people of Canada than it has been in the past. The Canadian Northern must shortly have a through line from the Pacific ocean down to Montreal and Quebec, it must get down to the sea-board in some way. I have an idea that in years to come, perhaps before long, the Intercolonial ought to get traffic from the Canadian Northern railway, its through traffic as well as its local traffic; and if the time ever comes when we have to release our arrangement with the Grand Trunk, which may not be for many years, then I think the proper thing for the Intercolonial would be to link up with the Canadian Northern railway, and hand its traffic from Montreal and Quebec, its through as well as its local traffic, over the Canadian Northern as far as possible for transportation west.
Now, I have talked altogether too long. The government railway is not easy to manage. I have to thank hon. members on both sides of the House for the_ courtesy that they have extended to those in charge of that railway. I live in a town in which are the Grand Trunk, the Canadian Pacific railway and Canadian Northern, and I know the applications which are made to members of parliament and the difficulties that arise sometimes in members being able to have matters adjusted exactly as they would like them to be, in the interest of the locality, and in the interest of the road as well. I have received a great deal of valuable advice from hon. members on both sides of the House, living along the line of railway not for the benefit of any particular individual, but for the benefit of the road and the people whom they represent. In future, we propose to manage the Intercolonial railway for the greatest benefit of the people who travel on it, or whose traffic is carried on it. I believe that the people of Canada have received great benefit from this road in the past and that in the future they will receive even greater benefit so long as we are able to manage it so that it will give them a good service at a reasonable rate and at the same time not put a burden upon the treasury of the Dominion government as it is not doing to any great extent at the present time.
In conclusion let me say, Sir, that there is no danger to Canadian transportation companies or our carrying trade, if we continue in the courageous course already outlined, and develop the national routes with which providence has endowed this country.

Mr. Speaker, it is rather late in the evening to commence a detailed reply to the remarks of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham). He perhaps could not help it, but I should judge Mr. GRAHAM.
that he was rather long in making his speech.
I agree absolutely.

It is not customary to present to the House the details in the form in which he gave them to us to-day. It is sufficient that they appear in the reports of his department without wearying the House with a continuous recital of details that it is impossible to consider or to answer at the time. The hon. gentleman began his remarks by pronouncing a eulogy upon the Board of Railway Commissioners. He said that they, were the finest body not only on this continent, but in the world, and perhaps the ablest. I do not know all these gentlemen, but I should judge they are fully competent for the positions which they fill. Their duties do not require the most ardent attention or the greatest ability, notwithstanding the statement of the hon. minister, but just such common sense as is requisite for the Minister of Railways and Canals himself. I think they have filled their positions well.
The hon. gentleman verged from that to the question of transportation. He stated that it was the important question of this country, that the tariff was a secondary consideration. I say that the two of them have to go together. In order that we may have transportation, we must carefully look after our tariff arrangements. I agree with the hon. gentleman to a certain extent with reference to what we must do with our canals. He has the modern idea. The modern idea is, that no railway transportation can compete successfully with water, that the two should go together that a railway along a river like the St. .Lawrence or the Mississippi is not a paradox. One is essential to the other. The very fact that by a waterway you can carry a certain line of freight in the cheapest manner, gives added value to the railway which parallels it. Railway companies in the United States are advocating the development of canal navigation along the line of their own railways for the purpose of handling such freight. That question has been most fully dealt with in Germany. The Germans are going ahead and developing what was thought a few years ago to be the antiquated system of canal .transportation for freight of a certain kind. In order to maintain our position on this continent, as the minister very well observes, we have to look after our transportation facilities. We are placed by nature in the most advantageous position of any nation on the continent of America. Nature has given us facilities for the development of our waterways superior to those of any other nation on this continent. We ought

to make full use of them because that nation through which the goods of another nation passes in going to market, virtually controls the political existence of the country which owns the goods. We are now in a position, if we maintain what we have at the present time, .to be the controllers of the destinies of that part of North America which lies along our beautiful water system. How can we best do it? The minister suggests two plans with reference to water communication-the building of the Welland canal and of the Georgian Bay canal. It is not
How happy could I be with either,
Were t'other dear charmer away.
with the Minister of Railways, but he loves both of them. He loves the banks of the St, Lawrence, and I do not blame him for favouring the development of what is to my mind, the most magnificent waterway in the world. To live on its banks is something^ because it is a beautiful river, but I must cease this flight of eloquence, and try to get down to something more practical. If the minister will take my advice, and I intend to give him reasons, he will be very careful about embarking upon an expenditure upon either of these great, undertakings without the fullest possible information. He has the fullest possible information as to what the Georgian Bay canal will cost, while he has not to such an extent information with reference to the St. Lawrence river and the cost of its improvement. I made a statement which I am prepared fto corroborate this evening, that the enlargement of the St. Lawrence canals to the capacity which is proposed-21 feet of navigation, or 24 feet on the mitre sills of the locks-will cost double the amount that will be required to build the Georgian Bay canal. Now, that is a strange statement. The building of that canal from the waters above to Lake Ontario, and, thence down to Montreal, will cost nearly .double what it would cost to build the Georgian Bay canal. I will give the figures and details with reference to this afterwards. What do you gain? The Georgian Bay canal route is 280 miles shorter than the other. It requires the most serious consideration why we should expend a large sum of money for making a ship canal down to Lake Ontario and from Lake Ontario to Montreal, if we do not require it.
We see in the newspapers that a proposition has been made to the Canadian government by the President of the United States for the joint - building of a canal from the St. Lawrence river to New York, and of course joint ownership. I am glad the minister has given no intimation that the government will pay heed to such . 161*
a proposal. We have got into trouble already by making an arrangement with the United States, and if you allow joint ownership of a single mile.or a single inch in our territory for the purpose of navigation, you might as well give the Americans the whole country. If they had joint ownership they would have the right to police it, and if they had the right to police it and line it with their troops, they would pretty soon own it. This government has had warnings enough and I do not think they need more, but I solemnly warn them not to enter into any arrangement of that kind. If it is necessary in the interests of the trade of the North American continent that a canal should be built, let us, poor as we are, build it ourselves. With 8,000,000 population we are in the position of the toad under the hat, but Sir, when we are 20,000,000 people in Canada, we can treat with any nation in the world on equal terms, which we do not at present. Let us keep to ourselves what belongs to us; let us keep our waterways and our navigation system for ourselves, and then we can virtually control the destiny of the whole North American continent. Now, to build the Georgian Bay canal it will we are told cost about $120,000,000 as estimated by the engineers.
A little over $100,000,000.

Well, we will put it at the extreme and say $120,000,000, and to build the new Welland canal into Lake Ontario, it would cost about $40,000,000. To build the Georgian Bay canal it would take about 12 years, and five 'years to build the other canal, the great cost of that work being the deepening and locking of the St. Lawrence river from Kingston to Montreal. The minister is right in having a thorough survey made. Time is a very important thing in transportation and if by any modern engineering device we can save hours and hours in locking, we will divert the traffic to that route. I would advise the minister to make the locks large and, although I do not know how the lift lock we have constructed, is working, something of that kind might be adopted to save time. If you are bound to build the Welland canal from Lake Erie to Lake Ontario, see that it is done on the best possible lines and on the most modern engineering principles. What is the object of getting freight from Lake Erie into Lake Ontario. If you have to scow it from Kingston down to Montreal cannot you carry it by boat or scow as easily as they do now from Port Colborne to Montreal. What is the great advantage of building a canal into Lake Erie unless you continue it down to ocean navigation. I can see no advantage for my part, and if the minister is going

to adopt that scheme the $5,000,000 we have spent on elevators and deepening the harbour at Port Colborne will be entirely wasted. That canal if built, will be a mutual benefit to Canadians and to Americans, and does the minister not realize what a large percentage of the traffic from west to east now goes via New York. That cannot be, because the facilities are not good in Montreal because we are told the capacity of Montreal harbour is two or three times greater than the present requirements. I believe, Sir, that the whole effort and energy of Canada should be directed towards intercommunication between the different portions of the Dominion. Without social intercourse, without commerce, without trade between the -different '(provinces you need not have a,Dominion at all. What we want to build up in the maritime provinces, in Quebec, and in Ontario, is a feeling of sympathy with the people of the Canadian west so that we may trade between each other, we taking as much as we can of their -surplus products, and they buying what we manufacture. Let us have a closer union between all the people of Canada so that we may build up on this northern part of the continent a strong and prosperous nation, which I believe to be the aspiration of every young man in this country. What was it that brought our fathers to the territory north of the St. Lawrence, cold and inhospitable as it was then thought, in comparison with the land they left. Why did they come here, if not with a determination that they and their children and their children's children should build up here a portion of that mighty British Empire of which they were so proud. And that Sir, I believe to be the destiny of the Canadian people.
That ought to be the object, and, as my hon. friend says, it can only be done by improving the means of intercommunication between the different parts of this Dominion. I will not trouble you with many details, but I would like to place upon ' Hansard ' my reasons for thinking that the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay canal will be a great benefit to the people of this country. The waterway will pass from Lake Huron at the northeast corner of the Georgian bay, and, following the French river, Lake Nipissing, the Mat-tawa and Ottawa rivers, will enter the St. Lawrence river at Montreal. In this manner connection will be made between the Great Lakes and the Atlantic ocean for large vessels up to 13,000 tons capacity. The canal will be 440 miles long, 22 feet deep, with a minimum width at the bottom of 200 feet. The rise and fall of the land will be overcome by 25 locks, each 650 feet long. I may state, too, that the whole of the excavation in this 440 miles will not be Mr. HAGGART (Lanark).
more than in the neighbourhood of about 25 miles. There may be a little dredging of 25 or 30 miles more, but the water between these excavations is deep, where a vessel can sail at full speed just as she can on the lakes. This was the route by which the people belonging to the Hudson Bay Company, Champlain and others travelled to the northwest; it was the old Indian route, and the shortest route from the east to the upper lakes and Hudson bay. I have not had the pleasure, like the hon. Minister of Railways, of living for any great length of time on the banks of the River St. Lawrence, but though I have a strong feeling of sympathy for that river, I am not speaking from sympathy, but from what I believe in my inmost soul to be in the interest of the people of this country, when I say that we shall never obtain the development we ought to obtain until we build that canal. I do not live near its banks. I am considering the future of this country, and the nation that commands that canal, secure from foreign interference unless by an act of war, will command the shortest possible route into the centre _ of this continent, and if we want to utilize our waterways we must build that canal. There is no railroad communication that can compete with water communication. You can carry freight by water for one-eighth per ton mile what you can by rail. It is the people's mode of transportation. It is true, companies may be formed to control transportation on water, as anywhere else, but any man can get a boat of his own. It is the mode of transportation that appeals to what the Minister of Finance speaks of as the horny-handed son of toil, as against the millionaire owner of railways and automobiles. Let us all unite to build this canal. It is not a political question, or one that ought to divide the parties in this House. We ought all to agree on some principle of developing this country. If we had used for this purpose some of the money that we have expended uselessly, as, for instance, the $50,000,000 which we have spent on capital account on the Intercolonial railway since 1897, the Georgian Bay canal would have been half finished at the present moment. This canal will give us, as I have _ said, a national waterway entirely within our own territory, far removed from the international boundary, and free from international complications, a waterway, which, under no conditions, can be used by the United States to assist them in wresting out of Canadian hands the trade of Canada's own Northwest, and it will secure, without possibility of competition. Canadian traffic for Canadian ports. It will foster existing and create new interprovincial trade both east and west, thus drawing closer the bonds of confederation and enormously increasing the national wealth and the power of the

[DOT]whole Dominion. It will greatly reduce the cost of carrying grain. It will open up Canadian Lake Huron and Lake Superior ports to Nova Scotia coal, thereby providing a market for a Canadian product to the extent of over 3,000,000 tons a year. It will very much assist the shipping of grain in winter. It will assist in the development of a million horse-power. As the hon. minister says,, the possession by the people of Canada of our enormous water-powers gives us the facilities for being the greatest manufacturing country in the world. There is no doubt the time will arrive when heat as well as power will be developed by electricity, and if we have no coal in this section of the country we have what is more than its equivalent, the power which will produce heat and everything else that coal will produce. Canada to-day is paying away to the United States millions of dollars annually, which ought to be retained in the country for the upbuilding of our own industries. If this is the case to-day, in a few years this state of affairs will be very much accentuated. Every Canadian will agree that Canadian grain exported to Europe should pass through Canadian channels, but what are the facts? In 1909, out of 56,000,000 bushels of Canadian-grown grain exported to Europe, 32,000,000 bushels, or 57 per cent, were carried over United States transportation routes for export at United States Atlantic seaports, which meant a loss to Canadian interests of over $2,000,000 for carriage alone. Why is this? There are many reasons. To state the matter briefly, the existing Canadian routes cannot handle this traffic either as cheaply, as quickly, or in such quantities as the United States routes can.
Take the St. Lawrence river route, this only carried in 1909, 18 per cent of the total grain exported from this country.
That is a disgrace to the country, a disgrace to the conditions of transportation in Canada. If it can be remedied only by the deepening of the St. Lawrence system, perfect that route, if it can be developed better by the plan I propose, build the Georgian Bay canal. I would not like to see the money of the country expended on that canal if I did not believe from the bottom of my heart that it is the cheapest, the best and the only plan by which we can control the exports of the Northwest, and of that part of the United States bordering on the Great Lakes.
We are paying to-day about $13,400,000 annually to the United States coal interests. The greatest portion of this could with proper transportation facilities be retained to our own people, although it might be necessary to put a higher duty on coal and that section of the country which I
represent would perhaps suffer the most. Utilize the water-powers we have in this section of the country, do everything that is necessary for the industrial life of the country, encourage the growth in Canada of the necessaries of life, the building of machinery, and the development of every industry that can properiy be carried on; finish all our products as nearly as possible to perfection before exporting them from this country. That is the policy that ought to be followed by this and every other government, and I thought it was the policy that was followed by my hon. friend. I might give reasons for the building of the Georgian Bay canal although the hour is late. But there is one thing that sticks out boldly and meets the view. We have surveys of the Georgian Bay canal, we know what it can be built for, we know that it will have the result of benefiting nearly every part of the country. It is not a party question, many of the foremost supporters of the project are on the minister's side of the House; let us unite and add one great scheme of water transportation from the Great Lakes. How the Americans see it! The President of the United States says that what is in the interest of the New York section of the country is the development of the waterways, and if possible the building up of oceanic communication, having ship communication between the Great Lakes and New York, if it is to retain even a moiety of the trade of that country. The Americans see that the only way to do this is not by building railways, but by the far cheaper mode of transportation with which Providence has so greatly favoured us, that of water communication. I earnestly entreat all my friends on both sides of the House-for I have arrived at the stage of life when I have no very bitter political opinions on any subject, I think perhaps good might come even from the Minister of Railways-and I ask him as I ask my friends on this side of the House to do all that they possibly can in developing what I think is of the greatest use to the people of this country.
The hon. gentleman talks about the Hudson Bay railway, and says he is going to-build it for the small amount of $20,000,000, I presume exclusive of terminals and steamboat communication between Canada and the old country. The minister must have a power in this House when they talk so lightly of an expenditure of $20,000,000 as nothing at all, and the manner in which my friend introduced it showed that he expected no opposition to it. If he wanted no opposition he should have had a different report laid on the table of the House. His deputy and the gentlemen who examined and surveyed that section of the country reported that they found a good enough

route nearly fulfilling the description of my friend the late Mr. Wood, who in discussing the building of the Canadian Pacific railway spoke of Manitoba as being amongst the eternal snows, still further up amongst the avalanches of the eternal snows where woman's sweet voice is never heard nor even the hum of the mosquito. I hope the event will be as opposite to my prophecy as the result of the building of the Canadian Pacific railway has been to Mr. Wood's. The minister's deputy says we may expect a full traffic on the road for a couple of months in the year, and a less amount for three months. He is very chary about what we will have for the remainder of the year. Has the minister, before making an expenditure of $25,000,000, considered how the cost is to be repaid to the people of this country? If it is a thing of benefit that the people of the Northwest expect in cheapening transportation and increasing the value of their farms and products I would have no objection to it. I do not know what the result may be, but I once applied with some others for a charter to build a railway from Winnipeg to Hudson bay. Looking at the map that seems an elegant thing. There were a couple of rival charters, and-we came to inquire into the navigation of Hudson bay. We found that the description was very much that of the deputy minister's report, that the navigation ends about October 15, and begins somewhere about the first of August. You would have two or three months of navigation during the year, but even two or three months, if possible and continuous, might be of immense benefit to the country. I remember when it. was thought that the navigation of the St. Lawrence would be only four or five months in the year.
I hope to see the day in the near future when, under the Minister of Marine and Fisheries we shall have ice breakers in the St, Lawrence, so that the river may be navigable at least as far up as Quebec for about eleven months of the year. I believe that it is quite possible. And I hope the navigation of Hudson bay will be found such that the evil forebodings of the present may be dissipated. However, the Hudson bay scheme is a large undertaking- $25,000,000 spent for a purpose which is still not beyond the range of doubt. I think the deputy minister says that it is the same distance from La Pas to Churchill as from Winnipeg to Lake Superior. The calculation was made, when I was Minister of Railways, that it would be cheaper to take grain down by the Canadian Pacific railway to Port Arthur, ship it by water to Montreal and thence to Great Britain than to take it by way of Hudson bay. It would cost about the same to leave grain on the shore of Hudson bay as to leave it at Port Mr. HAGGART (Lanark).
Arthur. The advocates of the Hudson bay scheme said: You will be in a better position by four cents a bushel than you are at Port Arthur; from Poi't Arthur to Montreal, it will cost you four cents a bushel, and it will cost you as much from Montreal to Liverpool as from Nelson or Churchill to Liverpool. But it will cost double as much to take grain from Churchill to Liverpool, under any system and with any equipment now known to navigation, as to take grain from Montreal to Liverpool. The minister says that the steamers can be employed for five months in the year. But it was thought in my time that it would require specially constructed steamers, and that they could not be profitably employed for more than three months in the year. That may not be true to-day. All that information the minister should be possessed of before he enters upon this expenditure of $25,000,000; and when he is fully satisfied he should see to it that the thing is done in a way to bring the best results for the people of the great and growing west. For the time will come, development proceeding as at present, when the exports of that country will be immensely in excess of what they are now; and every effort of the people of this country should be put forth in the direction of providing means to carry our surplus products to market. If these products are not to go down by Lake Superior and Montreal, St. John, Halifax and Quebec to the mother country, then, let them go by way of Hudson bay. In any case, let the transportation be over our own routes. As I said before, the country that controls transportation of the surplus products controls political destiny. If our surplus is to go to a foreign country to build up foreign transportation systems and industries, then we may say good-bye to the dreams of our young men for the building up of this country. Your regulations in reference to grain inspection, elevators, and transportation will be useless, for, in case of certain events, which, I hope in my soul will not come to pass, we shall not have a bushel of wheat to put into these elevators and your regulations will be idle wind. I was speaking to-day with a man who is engaged up to the eyes in industries of that kind, and he has come to the conclusion that the industries in which he has such large investments are worthless under certain conditions. But I hope for better things; I hope that something will happen in the meantime to save our country from the disaster which might overwhelm it. And I hope the Minister of Railways will use his influence in that direction. He seems to take an interest in these subjects and studies them up; I must say he does as well as I could expect him to do under the circumstances:	He does
very well anyway.
Now, a few words as to the Intercolonial railway. You must remember one thing

in making comparisons with the past, and that is that you have added $50,000,000 to the capital account of the Intercolonial since 1867. So, if you are making a comparison of two or three years back you should add interest on that $50,000,000. We were promised beautiful results from the acquisition of the Drummond railway with the large expenditure on capital account that was involved. The predecessor of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Graham) gave glowing accounts of how this railway was to be no longer a backwoods railway but was to be a first class road with its terminals in a first class city. And what has been the result' of all this? The minister does not even make mention of the past in this connection. And I think he is perfectly right, because after all, the people of Canada-certainly the young men of Canada-do not care a cent for anything that is more than four or five years old; they want something of the present and of the future, what the railway is doing and what it may be expected to do. The minister states that the Intercolonial affords the cheapest transportation of any railway on the continent. He makes comparisons with the Canadian Pacific railway, the Grand Trunk, the Canadian Northern, and, last of all with the Ontario system of railways. Does he think that a railway which has been in existence for about forty years should be compared in freight charges or anything else with a railway which has only been constructed and which is only struggling into existence as a backwoods road? Does he think that it is fair to make a comparison of freight and passenger rates with the Canadian Pacific railway? That road has a similar condition from Winnipeg to the Pacific coast. It is in great part what is called a mountain railway and has exceptional rates. And the Canadian Northern is in the same category. The only fair comparison is with the Grand Trunk. And the rates of freight on the Intercolonial, taking them all in all, are about the same as on the Grand Trunk. In all communications under twenty miles the passenger rates for both roads are prac-. tically the same.
I do not know the classification as to freights. What brings down the rate per ton per mile,- even in the classification on the Intercolonial, are two or three exceptional things. One is the carriage of coal, which we carry at the least possible rate for the purpose of fostering that industry. The other is the carriage of timber, sawn lumber and shingles, which are carried at a very low rate. But for ordinary traffic, I make the statement in this House that the rate for passenger traffic between way stations on the Intercolonial is as high as the ordinary charge on any other railway. It is as high as the New York Central, as high as the Erie, as high as the Grand Trunk. It is not as high on the whole as on the Canadian Pacific railway or the
Canadian Northern. The freight rates that apply in that country are fair freight rates, and so are the passenger rates. I think the minister ought to give other reasons for a shortage in the accounts, or for a failure to balance the two ends. There is one thing I am glad to see, and that is the prosperity in the maritime provinces, as shown by the traffic on the Intercolonial which they afford. In 1909 the collections amounted to $9,600,000, whereas the collections in 1897 were only about $3,000,000 a year. There must have been an enormous development in the wealth of the people of the maritime provinces to enable them to pay to the Intercolonial railway the amount they are now paying in collections.
The minister says that the railway is handicapped by water competition. Water communication* between two points develops a trade which railroads cannot do, because you can carry freight by water communication for one-eighth of what it costs to carry it by railway. If you are to build up industries, if you are to develop the resources of that country, you must have cheap com-muni cat ion, a cheap communication which the railroads cannot give. I congratulate the minister on the better showing the Intercolonial is making. It is to the interest of the people of Canada that that road should be prosperous, and that the maritime provinces should be prosperous. It is more necessary now than ever that the central and western provinces should have the closest alliance with our sister provinces down by the sea. The fate of this Dominion depends upon the existence of a similarity of ideas between the people of middle and western Canada with the inhabitants of the maritime provinces. This is_ absolutely necessary to enable us to build up the nationality on which we have all set our hearts. Mr. Speaker, I have a good many more things that I wish to say, and 1 may take another opportunity of outlining my scheme for the development of transportation in Canada.

I trust that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hag-gart) who has just taken his seat will not regard me as displaying any lack of courtesy if I fail to follow him in his remarks. Let me say that I share with him in his enthusiasm for the development of a transportation system in this country. I join with the greatest pleasure in his support of the construction of the Georgian Bay canal, which I think deserves immediate consideration at the hands of the government, and which is absolutely necessary in the interests of every part of this country. I am sure the House listened with a great deal of pleasure to the remarks of the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart) in his review of the condition of the Intercolonial railway. On this side of the House we all regard with the greatest respect the vener-

able representative of Lanark, who in days past has filled the position of Minister of Railways, and who enjoys in a high degree the esteem and respect of those who sit on the right hand of the Speaker.
Now, let me refer briefly to some phases of the situation in regard to the Intercolonial as outlined by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham). Let me say, as I said last year, that I think the surplus which the minister makes out as somewhere in the vicinity of $700,000, is about $650,000 too large, and I will give my reason for saying so. It is a reason not generally understood at first sight; but let me point out that when you make a comparison in the operation of the Intercolonial with the operation of any company road in this country, there is a marked difference between the application of the revenues. At the close of the financial year of any company, if they have a surplus of a million or two, that money is available during the succeeding year for the purpose of renewals, extensions or repairs which are necessary in the interest of revenue. Not so in the case of the Canadian government railway. On the 31st of March next it will be the duty of the accountant of the Railway Department to place to the credit of the Receiver General of this Dominion that surplus of $700,000. It has gone forever from the Intercolonial, it is not available in the succeeding year for any purpose for the improvement of the road. The reason I say that the surplus of $650,000 is too large, is for that reason to begin with, but let me give you another reason. The Intercolonial railway was an interprovincial work. As my hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) well knows, it was one of the propositions that was essential at the time of confederation, include'd in the British North America Act as one qf the very conditions upon which these four prov-[DOT] inces decided to group themselves together to form the nucleus which was in time to be the Canada of to-day. It was not on account of it benefiting merely the people of the maritime provinces that the expenditure for that road was contemplated or made, but it was made for the unity and benefit of Canada as a whole. When you come to consider the Intercolonial railway you are coming to deal with a proposition which intrinsically differs from that of any other railway in the Dominion. Had you had no Intercolonial railway you never would have had any confederation. It is at the very basis of the whole system, quite as essential as one of the corner stones of the edifice which was afterwards constructed as any of the other provisions fought for and discussed at great length in arriving at the terms of the British North America Act. It is in the same position as the canals which were constructed in the central portion of Canada and which were then taken over. It was what the tran-Mr. MACDONALD.
sportation system by water was to the centre of Canada; it was essential that we should have communication with the different parts of Canada in order to make confederation a possibility.
The minister has told us the amount which has been expended upon the Intercolonial railway since that time, and which is somewhere in the vicinity, according to the last railway returns, of $82,000,000. During the same period there has been expended $96,000,000 on account of the canals. I am aware that this argument has been made before in this House, but I may be pardoned if I refer to it again. There is this difference, that while nobody in this country expects any revenue from the canals, while they are run absolutely free, while no tolls are charged on the traffic that goes through them, and nobody wants to have tolls charged, we have this remarkable fact that it is regarded as a sin and a disgrace that the minister does not come in and announce a great big surplus on the Intercolonial railway. For that reason, and on account of these conditions, the surplus is altogether too large. If government ownership is of any value, why should it be that the people who are operating a government utility, and more particularly a government utility of that peculiar character, it being an ante-confederation essentia], be expected to show a large surplus? That $650,000 of a surplus cannot be psed for capital expenditure if it is _ not spent before the 31st of March of this year, it goes into the treasury and is voted out again by way of capital, if not for revenue. Now. it is a gratifying thing, as the ex-minister has said, that the development of the maritime provinces has produced a condition of affairs in which the road has a revenue three times what it was worth fourteen or fifteen years ago. The extension of the road from Quebec to Moncton was one of the essential things which contributed to that condition. The original road consisted of the smallest kind of a local proposition, ending at Riviere du Loup. Gradually it was extended to Quebec; only within the last twelve years has it run to Montreal, and even to-day it is a local road. It does not share in any of the advancement which has come to western Canada, or to the largest province in the Dominion-Ontario. We never tap directly any part of your business, simply because, when it comes to Montreal, the Intercolonial railway can only get what the Grand Trunk railway or the Canadian Pacific railway give it, and what it gathers from the other railways, local or large as they may be. Being only a local road on that account, that the country should be clamouring for a surplus of half a million, or of any amount, is altogether absurd. It seems to me that

the proper view to take of this proposition Is that if this road is run so that both ends meet and the country is not called upon to contribute anything for any deficit that may arise you have a proper condition of affairs with regard to the Intercolonial railway. The minister deserves to be congratulated upon the intelligent appreciation of events from the railway standpoint which he	has displayed in	dealing	withrailways.	But there are	one	or	twothings to	which I want	to	call	hisattention.	It is no answer	for	my	hon.
friend the Minister of Railways, or for myself as the representative of a constituency supporting him, to go to a district in my county which has had a telegraph station for the last twenty-five years, and which was closed up a year ago, and say: It is true that you have had your station closea up and you have not now the facilities which you have had for twenty-five years, but we have a surplus of $700,000, which goes into the treasury, and which is no good to the Intercolonial railway after March 31. I say that there is a situation where my hon. friend could use a surplus. That is a simple ease. Why take away the facilities which have existed in the past, when, by this small expenditure, the whole country would not be affected in any way whatever, and you would have a substantial condition under which both ends would meet?
With regard to the question of freights, my hon. friend the minister produced figures which, as the ex-Minister of Railways says, require a good deal of study to ascertain just what they really mean. There has been an increase of freights on the Intercolonial Tailway in the last three or four years. With regard to certain local freights for short distances, the freight rates are rather too onerous. It must be remembered that the real manufacturing, or producing, portion of the Intercolonial railway is the extreme eastern part of it, and that there are intermediate agricultural districts which do not produce exportable manufactured articles, or any articles upon which high classification exists. Therefore, it is difficult to make a comparison with the business of other railways, or to ascertain accurately just how these rates work out when applied to the trade of the people who use the railway the most. But it does seem to me, having regard to the premise that I have attempted to lay down and having regard to all the conditions, that it should not be expected that a surplus should be obtained from this Toad. It may be said it is an anomaly that a representative of the people should stand up in parliament and say with regard to an important public utility that you should find fault with the size of the surplus. But Sir, I seriously contend that the proposition I make is absolutely sound, and that it
cannot be questioned from any reasonable standpoint.
There is another thing with regard to the administration of the road that I would like to take the opportunity of referring to. The men who are working on the Intercolonial railway are servants of the Crown, and they ought to be treated as servants of the Crown. When increases in wages are to be given they should be given by the government through the minister, and by the minister through his officials, having proper regard to the best administration of the road. The minister should not give assent to the proposition that conciliation boards would be appointed for the determination of such questions on the Intercolonial railway. Not long ago I was told by the government in answer to a question, a fact which I well knew, that there was no statute which provided for a conciliation board in connection with the Intercolonial railway. Suppose that in the Marine Department the right of the servants of the Crown to strike is recognized (and that is the basis of the Conciliation Act), and you are going to assume they will strike, by appointing a conciliation board, (which is another feature of the Conciliation Act), you have from every standpoint of the administration of the law a most anomalous position. Suppose our friends the men of our fishery cruisers made up their minds when they came to port that they were not getting enough wages, and some enterprising gentleman who was interested in promoting these boards came along and said: Demand an increase of wages from the minister, and if he does not give it have a conciliation board, and the whole operation of the ships was dependent upon the decision of that board, how absurd the situation would be. But it is no more absurd than it is in the case of the Intercolonial railway, because every man working on the Intercolonial railway is a servant of the Crown, and he accepts employment as such, and if he wants to have the advantages which accrue from company operation of a road he should seek employment on a company road. The responsibility of determining what should be done in regard to the servants of the Crown whether employed on a railway or elsewhere, should be exercised by the responsible minister. Suppose the minister had to announce to parliament that by reason of a decision of a conciliation board which compelled him to pay $100,000 more to a certain class of employees there was a deficit on the road, parliament would have a perfect right to say that the minister had no business to accept the decision of such a board, because it does not bind parliament.
Could not the minister delegate his powers to a conciliation bofird and ask it to make inquiry?

That is another thing altogether. I say that the minister acting through his commission who are the best judges in this matter ought in proper cases to increase the salaries of the employees, and whether he did so or not he should assume the responsibility. There is another thing in connection with this comparison between the Intercolonial railway and the Canadian Pacific railway, and the Grand Trunk railway; the Canadian Pacific railway and the Grand Trunk railway have ocean connections, they have steamers in connection with their railway, they have booking agencies in Europe and every facility for inducing passengers to take their lines, all of which the Intercolonial railway does not possess. Our industries in the maritime provinces seriously complain that ocean steamers will carry iron and steel and other commodities from Liverpool right across the ocean and as far west as Toronto, and that the freight including steamer and railway will be less than the industries in the maritime provinces have to pay for the transportation of similar articles for the land journey alone. Why that should be I do not know, but it is a thing the minister should look into.
Did we not give the commission power to control the rates on railways and ocean connections?

Not the steamship rates. The question was discussed, but it never was legislated upon. Now, in the last parliament attention was directed to a proposition that the British preference should bp extended to only such goods as were brought to Canada through Canadian ports, and hon. gentlemen opposite who three or four years ago took strong ground against that because they wished to get their goods through New York and Boston rather than through Halifax and St. John in winter are the men who to-day are very much excited about the danger to Canadian autonomy and Canadian loyalty, because they claim that under the agreement with the United States goods are likely to go through American ports. These are the men who four years ago opposed a resolution proposed in this parliament by a Nova Scotia member which said that the British preference should only be given to goods which came in through Canadian ports. If, such a regulation were put in force and Canadian imports went through the maritime province ports in winter we would have an advantage for the Intercolonial railway which we have never had since it was built.

The maritime ports were objected to because when goods were landed in them, it was two weeks before they Mr. HAGGART (Lanark).
reached upper Canada. I know that from my own experience. I shipped my goods for many years through New York and Boston simply on account of the delay in the lower Canadian ports. That was the whole trouble.
I do not feel like giving to my hon. friend from London the retort I might.
Do not be afraid.

There are some gentlemen so excited about sending goods through American ports that their loyalty ought surely to be strong enough to permit them to wait a week or two in order to get their goods through Canadian ports.
Sometimes three weeks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What is three weeks for the sake of the old flag?
I have been in the field sixteen weeks for the flag. If you are in business, and your customers want goods, and you cannot get them by one route you must have them brought in by the other.

I do not want to be turned into that discussion, further than to say that I hope that our good friends on the other side will now be found supporting us on this side when we ask the government to put into effect legislation which will give us trade through Canadian ports not only in summer, but for the whole twelve months of the year and satisfied they can get them as quickly through our ports as through New York or Boston. That it seems to me would afford one solution of the Intercolonial railway problem.
Why did not the government, who had the majority behind them, put it into effect?

Because certain business interests of the country, some of whom are allied very closely with my hon. friend and his associates, represented that it would be such an injury to them that the government did not carry out the request made to them by gentlemen on this side of the House. If the jion. gentleman looks at ' Hansard/ he will find the names of the gentlemen who made that complaint.
Some of the Toronto gentlemen who are making_the greatest noise now came to me and asked me not to do it, as they wanted their goods to come in by way of New York.

I am speaking as a Canadian who comes from -..the maritime provinces, and I say that the problem of

railway transportation in this country will not be solved until we see the necessity of applying that preference so as to give the advantage to Canadian ports the whole year round. Following the same line, I think that many of these discussions in parliament would be saved and a great many heart-burnings on the question of the Intercolonial railway would be avoided, if our transcontinental systems were extended to the extreme limit of Canada and were permitted to operate on the lines of railway which are now called the Intercolonial. In the statute which provides for the construction of the Transcontinental railway, there is a covenant under which running rights over the Intercolonial from Moncton east, are accorded to the Grand Trunk Pacific upon arrangements to be effected. Here is the Canadian Pacific railway at St. John, and we have on our Atlantic coast, some 200 or 300 miles nearer to Liverpool, available ports which can be reached at all seasons of the year without any difficulty. Therefore, it seems to me that it would be in the interests ofdDana-dians that the Canadian Pacific railway should also be given the right to run freight and passenger trains over the.,rails of the Intercolonial railway under conditions fair to the country and to the company. If in this way we had immediate connection with the various transcontinental lines, so that a man in the extreme east of Canada could go on any one of our transcontinental lines to the extreme west, and come back on any one of them without that dislocation which necessarily exists as an impediment to traffic when you have to transfer from one railway to another, and go into the division of payments and the allocations of freight incident thereto, it seems to me that the maritime provinces would be satisfied, and the whole interests of Canada would be advanced.
We had that in 189?. The Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific railway both had running rights over the Intercolonial.

I think my hon. friend must be mistaken. The Canadian Pacific railway trains still run on the Intercolonial between St. John and Halifax, under a working arrangement with the government; but these are really government railway trains making connection with the Canadian Pacific railway at St. John.

The hon. gentleman will remember that the late Mr. Blair, when Minister of Railways, pointed out the monstrosity of the agreement which the late government had made with the Canadian Pacific railway, giving it running power over the Intercolonial to Halifax.
They took the cream of the local traffic.
According to the Minister of Railways, there is no cream down there.

I am one of the younger men who look to the future rather than to the past, and I trust that the minister will regard favourably the proposition which I make, which would afford the people of my province the advantages of these transcontinental railway systems. From the point of view of trade and transportation, an immediate connection with the various transcontinental lines operated through the whole of Canada would be an advantage which it is desirable to obtain if it is possible to obtain it on fair terms.

I do not intend to deal with any of the questions that have been dealt with by the Minister of Railways, or those who have followed him. The railway question is. a very important question in western Canada. Ever since I have been in this -/House I have not been in sympathy with the' methods that are employed here in the granting .of railway charters. I remember very distinctly my first visit to the Railway Committee, a little over two years ago, when certain interests were looking for a charter for a railway through the constituency which I represent in this House. I remember asking the gentleman who had charge of the Bill, what his clients proposed doing, when they proposed doing it, and the amount of money they proposed expending. He was very emphatic in his answers. He told me that they were going to commence work at a very early date, that they practically had the money arranged for. I suggested that it would not be amiss to ask those interested to put up say 5 per cent as a guarantee of good faith1.. The committee did not, however, appear to see eye to eye with me in that respect. Now, I have heard it said in this House that we should not demand from people applying for railway charters any evidence of their good intentions-that there was free trade in railway charters.
Now, I wish to point out to the House the situation in the west. Settlers are going many miles from railway lines. They learn of these charters being granted, and the moment they are granted they begin to look forward to the construction of the roads, and it is easily understood that they are disappointed when year after year passes by and they do not get any portion of the roads for which the charters have been granted. Those interests come back here and get renewals of charters. I remember asking two years ago for a return showing the mileage for which railway charters

were granted outside of the three active railway-builders in this country. Between the years 1900 and 1907 we granted charters for a total mileage of something like 37,000 miles, of which something in the neighbourhood of 400 miles were constructed. In the first session that I was here, two years ago, we dealt with some 56 charters, of which 43 were renewals, and 13 new applications. Last year we dealt with 52 charters; 37 were renewals and 15 new applications. I understand that there is a Bill before the Senate which is designed to improve that situation. It appears to me that the question of improving the method of granting charters in this country is a matter that should be dealt with entirely by the government. After the charter is granted the next move is for the railway company to file its route map. That is done with the Department of Railways, i have been present when the Minister of Railways has dealt with these route maps, and I must say, in fairness to him, that he deals fairly with those who come before him. The moment, however, that these route maps are approved, the information goes back to the. country where the people are and then they believe, knowing the procedure which is that the maps of location have to be filed with the Railway Department and that these plans cannot depart more' than one mile from the line as shown on the route map, they believe they know where that railway is to be constructed, they make their plans, they have been known to buy land and locate along the line where the route is shown on the route map and then we have instances in which these active railway corporations, I know that the Canadian Northern, and I know that the Canadian Pacific railway have come back with amended plans which they present to the Minister of Railways for reconsideration. The minister gives us notice and we are permitted to be present at the time, but in that immense country it is impossible to get at the people in sufficient time to see to what extent they have been led to locate along the line as shown upon the route map. No railway company can undertake to lay down a route on a map from which they cannot deflect more than one mile without making a survey of that route, and I say that something should be done to give these railways to understand that when they come here with their route maps for approval these route maps have to stand or if they are to be allowed to change their route maps and have them amended from time to time I think it would be better to do away with route maps altogether. I know two or three cases where serious injury has been done to individuals in that way, the route map has been changed some six or seven miles. I feel that it is my duty to bring this matter to the attention of the minister in the way I am now doing.
Mr. MAGiRATH.
I would say a few words on the general question of railway development in western Canada. What is the situation, for instance, in, southern Alberta, and all over the west. We invite settlers to come into that country; they take up our lands, they go very many miles from railways in order to get those lands. The constant cry which I have been receiving from my constituency ever since I have been in this House has been: When are we to receive better railway facilities? Had I known this question was coming up I would have collected some of these letters and placed them on record. We have three active railways operating in that country. They bring into the country large sums for the building of railways. I claim that the railway mileage is not distributed over that country so as to do the greatest good to the greatest area in the shortest possible time. No one would question that statement who knows anything about the situation in that country. I claim that these railways are, to a certain extent, jockeying each other. One railway comes into a certain locality, and the two others appear to think it is necessary that they should come in and run alongside of it. I claim that we have railways bonused, or with bonds guaranteed by the people, running within two or three miles of each other. My view is that as one railway invades a certain territory the other comes in behind it, and possibiy the third behind that, and if by any accident there should be a few townships left the first loops back and gets in behind the other two. That is a problem the Department of Railways might take hold of. I see no reason why the Minister of the Interior, who is looking after the lands in that country, should not associate himself with the Minister of Railways and get the heads of the active railways here at the beginning of the year and discuss with them their plans for the current year, and by that means endeavour to get them to spread their energies over a larger territory. For instance, in southern Alberta the Canadian Pacific railway is in the best position to, in a measure, meet the needs of that part of the west, whilst in some other parts of the country the Grand Trunk would be best able to supply better facilities, and the Canadian Northern, in all probability, could pick up another section of country. Then, when these roads had fairly met the needs of the several districts, they could invade the territory of each other as fully as they wished. I venture to question if the Minister of Railways, having given us vast masses of statistics here to-day is in a position to cite to this House what' the Canadian Pacific railway is going to build in the prairie provinces this year, or the Canadian Northern, or the Grand

Trunk Pacific. I have been here for two years, and I have never been able to get information of that character. It is all very well to be looking over our shoulder at the past and gathering information of the character we have been receiving today from the minister I would like to see more interest taken by looking into the future and knowing something of what these roads propose doing and where. They receive charters from the people. I am not here as being opposed to railway corporations. I believe in bringing the railways and the people together. The farmers cannot do without the railway any more than the railway can do without the farmers. The cry of the farmer in the west is that he is not getting proper attention in that respect. I hope that the minister will take my suggestions in the spirit in which they are given. This is not a political question at all, and I merely say I feel we should know more about what these railway companies are doing, and I see no reason why the government should not. at the beginning of each year, find out from those roads what they are doing, and at the same time endeavour to pull them apart thereby distributing their energies, because looking at their work in the west, it appears that they appear to wish to run in the same channel.

Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
Progress reported.
